summary.title: Every way to make it harder
points: Progression isn't only more weight.
Options: reps, sets, slower lowering, pauses, range, harder variation, one side, less rest, load.
Choose one method per exercise per block.
Default: reps then load; the others when the weight jump is too big.

options: A 3-second lowering phase on every rep
Slower lowering with the same dumbbells
questions.explanation: The others work with what you have.

options: Nothing; more methods always means faster progress
questions.explanation: One method per exercise per block.

options: Load first, every session, whatever happens

summary.title: Double progression
points: Use a rep range, e.g. 8–12.
Keep the weight and add reps until every set hits the top with ≥1 in reserve.
Then add weight and start near the bottom.
With big jumps, use a wider range (10–15 or 12–20).
The load helper applies the rules.

exercises.scenario: Range 8–12. Last session at 10 kg: 12, 12, 11.

options: Move to 12 kg now, since two sets reached the top
Drop to 8 kg to make the reps easier
Add a fourth set at 12 kg
questions.explanation: Not every set has reached the top.

questions.prompt: Then all three sets hit 12 with 2 in reserve. Next?
options: Move up two weights at once
Stay at 10 kg for another four weeks
Move up and start near 8 reps

options: A narrower range, like 6–8, to force the jump

questions.prompt: What does the load helper need?
options: Only your body weight and age
Range, weight, reps per set, RIR and available weights

summary.title: When the next weight is too heavy
points: 10 → 12.5 kg is 25%; 12 → 16 kg is 33%: often too big.
Reps of about 0.5–8 s built similar muscle; very slow reps (> ~10 s) may be less effective.
Bridge: more reps, slower or paused reps, one side or harder version, then the heavier weight for 1 set, then 2.
If nothing works, buy kit (Module 3).

options: Stop rowing until you buy a 14 kg bell
Go straight to 16 kg for all sets and accept fewer reps
Keep adding reps up to about 20
16 kg for the first set only, then two sets
16 kg for five sets the next day

options: Very slow reps may build less muscle
Slower is always better for muscle, without any limit

summary.title: A one-minute log
points: Log date, exercise, weight, reps per set, RIR on the last set, a note.
Weekly review: what progressed, what stalled 2–3 sessions, sleep and energy.
Then set next week's targets.
Keep it light: one line per exercise.

exercises.scenario: You write today's log.

options: 'Good session, felt strong, legs tired, nice weather'
questions.explanation: Weight, reps per set and effort.

questions.prompt: When do you review the log?
options: Only at the end of the year, all at once

options: Nothing; logs only matter for professionals
A need to switch programmes immediately

questions.prompt: Which part of the training loop is the weekly review?
options: Plan, which comes before any training

summary.title: Fatigue and deloads
points: Deload: a period of reduced training stress to shed fatigue and prepare (2023 Delphi consensus).
Practice: every 4–8 weeks, about one week.
Same exercises and weights, about half the sets, 3–4 reps in reserve.
Warning signs: performance down two sessions in a row, poor sleep, lingering joint aches.

exercises.scenario: Week 6: two lifts dropped two sessions running and sleep is poor.

options: Add sets to push through the dip

questions.prompt: What does the deload week look like?
options: Same exercises and weights, about half the sets
New exercises at maximum effort to keep things fresh

exercises.scenario: A friend says deloads are for elite lifters only.

questions.prompt: What do they do for anyone?
options: Reduce accumulated fatigue and prepare for the next block
Nothing; recreational lifters never accumulate fatigue

questions.prompt: Is one bad session a reason to deload?
options: Yes, always take a month off
Yes; any bad session means a full deload week
No; look for a pattern over two or three
questions.explanation: One bad day isn't a pattern.

summary.title: Plateaus
points: Plateau: no progress on a lift for 2–3 weeks despite consistent training.
Check: effort, sleep and stress, food, weekly volume, fatigue.
Only then change the exercise or rep range.
In a deficit, holding strength can be a win.

exercises.scenario: Push-ups stalled for three weeks during a 900 kcal-a-day deficit.

options: Push-ups stop working after a month for everyone

questions.prompt: What do you check first in any plateau?
options: The brand of your dumbbells and the mat
Effort: are sets really 1–3 from failure?
questions.explanation: Effort is first on the list.

exercises.scenario: A friend changes programme every time a lift stalls.

options: Programme first, then everything else if that fails
Effort, sleep, food, volume, fatigue, then programme

questions.prompt: How should you judge progress during fat loss?
options: Strength held, plus waist and photos
Only by new personal bests every week
questions.explanation: Holding strength in a deficit is progress.

summary.title: Changing exercises
points: Planned variation can help; excessive random variation may compromise gains (2022 review).
Keep main lifts 6–12 weeks; rotate accessories freely.
Change a main lift when it stalls despite the checklist, hurts, or kit allows better.
Swap within the same pattern.

options: Never change any exercise at all
A brand-new set of exercises every single session
questions.explanation: You can still progress the main lifts.

questions.prompt: Goblet squats stalled despite the checklist. Swap to?
options: Push-ups, to give the legs a complete break

exercises.scenario: Social media says 'muscle confusion' needs daily new workouts.

options: Daily variation is required to keep any muscle growing
Variation has no effect either way
Excessive random variation may compromise gains

questions.prompt: How long should a main lift stay?
options: One session only, to keep the body guessing

summary.title: How to progress
points: Many ways to progress: reps, sets, tempo, pauses, range, variation, one side, density, load.

Big jumps: widen the range and bridge with reps, tempo, pauses or one side.
Useful tempo is about 0.5–8 s per rep.

Plateau checklist: effort, sleep, food, volume, fatigue, then programme.
Keep main lifts 6–12 weeks; rotate accessories.

Replace every exercise in the programme straight away

questions.prompt: Describe how you'll progress your goblet squat over the next 8 weeks.
questions.modelAnswer: Range 10–15 at 12 kg: add reps each session until all sets reach 15 with a rep or two in reserve; then bridge to 16 kg (more reps or slower lowering, then 16 kg for one set, then two, then all), logging every session and deloading around week 6–8 if needed.
